title: I've been coding for 15 years and used AI on my game – why I'm still hesitant to use the "AI-assisted code" tag
author: sir_t9awed
selftext:
I'm not against AI, and I'm not against using it in productive ways. What I'm against is slop and lazy content in general, whether it comes from a human or from AI. Something being made with AI doesn't automatically make it worse than something made by a person.

The main reason I'm hesitant to put the "AI-assisted code" tag on my game is simple: I'm afraid of mass dislikes or review bombs purely because of the politics around it right now.

I also think game development shouldn't be gatekept so that only people who know how to code (or who can turn complex abstract ideas into code) get to make games. That feels unfair to anyone with a clear vision but no programming background. If you've got the budget, you can just hire coders and ship a game. To me that isn't fundamentally different from using AI as a tool. Kojima isn't primarily a programmer (he knows basic programming and scripting, but he's not writing the engine himself). He leads teams of programmers. Those programmers are talented, but they probably wouldn't have made the games we associate with him without his direction. That's why I sometimes think "game designer" is a more accurate description than "game developer" for a lot of people in this space.

I've been a programmer for over 15 years. I started when I was 13 with Flash, then moved into basic bash and spent years tinkering with whatever I could get my hands on. I've never actually published a game on my own, but I've done game jams with friends and colleagues. I can confidently say I could have written 100% of the code for this project myself without AI. I just didn't want to. Anyone who has done any real amount of programming knows how much of it is boilerplate. In most cases the actual "secret sauce" is a few hundred lines at most. The rest is repetitive work. Code has always been reused and recycled. Since around 2010 I've been reusing other people's code and sharing my own snippets. I still remember the day I discovered Stack Overflow. The amount of high-quality code that people just put out there for free made it feel like I could suddenly build almost anything.

On this game I still wrote most of the code myself, but I used autocomplete and Copilot. I also handed a lot of the pure boilerplate off to agents. The time it saved is hard to overstate. The same project would have taken me about two years without AI, and probably longer once you factor in the procrastination and demotivation that hits when you know you have to wire up a bunch of UI, build a save/load system, or deal with 150 sound effects and voice lines. The core game mechanics were 100% designed and implemented by me. I only had AI review them afterward for bugs and optimization. The time I got back went into art direction, building a specific vibe, curating assets, and polishing every detail the player actually interacts with. Everything the AI generated was reviewed by me, and I caught and fixed a few mistakes. That review process is still far less tedious and time-consuming than writing all of it from scratch.

My larger point is that game development shouldn't be limited to people who can code from first principles. Computers used to be limited to people who knew how to use a terminal. That eventually changed because better interfaces showed up. AI is, in a lot of ways, just a new interface for working with software and creating things. What actually separates good work from bad work is attention and design quality. That distinction exists whether the tools involved are AI or not. Plenty of fully human-made games (including some AAA ones) have been absolute dogshit.

I get why some people hate AI. Mass layoffs, art and copyright issues, and other concerns are real. A lot of that is debatable, and I'm not going to get into those arguments here. I'm mostly talking about the practical side of using the tools while still being the one who has to care about the result, and about not wanting the politics to decide how the game is received before anyone even plays it.
